patches.find: Roughly 12,500 Confederate soldiers advanced across nearly a mile of open ground against the Union center. A small group under Brigadier General Lewis Armistead breached the low stone wall at 'the Angle' before being overwhelmed. The assault failed with over 50% casualties among the attacking force.
patches.repl: A Confederate column that Hancock estimated at more than 15,000 men advanced across nearly a mile of open ground against the Union center. A part of Brigadier General Lewis Armistead's brigade breached the low stone wall at 'the Angle' before being overwhelmed. The assault failed with heavy loss: the Confederate return counts 2,888 casualties in Pickett's division alone.
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.373; OR 27/2 p.339

patches.find: "panel_summary": "At approximately 7:30am on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry fired the first shot of the Battle of Gettysburg. He borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail, and fired at a distant Confederate officer. The shot missed -- but 51,000 casualties would follow."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "About 7:30 a.m. on July 1, 1863, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones of the 8th Illinois Cavalry is traditionally credited with the first shot of the battle, fired from a borrowed carbine at a Confederate officer on the Chambersburg Pike. Other men claimed earlier shots, so the claim is contested; the Official Records credit Lieutenant Roder's gun of Calef's battery with the first artillery shot."
patches.note: contested-fact: time-facts R005 (HistoryNet, Stone Sentinels, NPS marker); OR 27/1 p.1031 (Calef); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth, 5 a.m.)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The morning of July 1 was warm and hazy when Corporal Alphonso Hodges spotted movement on the Chambersburg Pike. He reported to his sergeant: Confederate infantry, coming in force.

Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding the vedette post of Company E, 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed Sergeant Levi Shafer's carbine. He rested the barrel on a fence rail along the Knoxlyn Ridge. In the distance, perhaps 700 yards away, a mounted Confederate officer rode along the pike ahead of his advancing column.

Jones squeezed the trigger.

The shot missed. The officer rode on. But the sound of that single shot rolled across the fields and into the histories of both nations.

It was approximately 7:30 in the morning. The Battle of Gettysburg had begun.

Jones had no way of knowing what his missed shot had set in motion. He could not know that 51,000 men would become casualties on this ground over the next three days. He could not know that the shot he had just fired -- borrowed, aimed from a fence rail, and wasted -- would be commemorated by a monument that still stands on Knoxlyn Ridge today.

He rode back to report what he had seen. Behind him, Heth's Confederate division continued its march toward Gettysburg."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Buford's pickets west of Gettysburg watched Heth's division come down the Chambersburg Pike on the morning of July 1. By tradition, Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding a vedette post of the 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed a carbine from a sergeant, rested it on a fence rail and fired at a Confederate officer riding ahead of the column, at about 7:30 in the morning. A monument on the pike marks the place the tradition names.

Not everyone agrees. Men of other regiments later claimed to have fired first, some of them hours earlier; the account that examined those claims found them mistaken, because Heth's column had barely left Cashtown at five o'clock. Artillery has its own claim: in his report Lieutenant Calef of Battery A, 2nd U.S. Artillery, writes that 'Lieutenant Roder now fired the first gun (which opened the sanguinary battle of Gettysburg)' on the head of a column of Confederate cavalry.

Behind the shot Heth's division, which he says was ordered to move at 5 a.m., marched on toward Gettysburg."
patches.note: contested-fact: time-facts R005 (HistoryNet, Stone Sentinels, NPS marker); OR 27/1 p.1031 (Calef); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth, 5 a.m.)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Major General John Reynolds, the finest corps commander in the Army of the Potomac, was killed at approximately 10:15am while personally leading the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods. Shot through the head, he fell dead from his horse. He was 42 years old. His death left a void in Union command that was never truly filled."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Major General John F. Reynolds, commanding the left wing of the Army of the Potomac, was killed on the morning of July 1 as the Iron Brigade went into McPherson's (Herbst) Woods. Doubleday gives the hour as about 10:15 a.m., Howard's reports give 11:15, and the source of the shot is unsettled."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/1 p.114 (Meade), p.245 (Doubleday: "about 10.15 a. m."), p.696 (Howard 11.15), p.702, p.727 (11.30); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth); ledger WSD-14. The offer of army command was Lincoln's, not Meade's, and is dropped

patches.find:
"full_script": "John Fulton Reynolds was, by nearly universal agreement, the best corps commander in the Army of the Potomac. Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier. Reynolds had refused -- he wanted the freedom to fight without political interference. He had ridden ahead of his corps to Gettysburg that morning to see the situation for himself.

What he saw at the Seminary convinced him that the Union army had to fight here. He sent a courier galloping south: bring the I Corps forward at the double-quick. And then, because Reynolds was that kind of general, he did not wait at the Seminary. He rode forward to lead the attack himself.

The Iron Brigade -- his beloved Iron Brigade -- was double-quicking across the fields toward the dark woods of Herbst. Reynolds rode to their head. He waved them forward into the trees, shouting encouragement.

The shot came without warning.

It struck Reynolds behind the right ear. He fell from his saddle without a word. By the time his aides reached him, he was already dead.

He was 42 years old. He had never married. He had been engaged to a woman named Kate Hewitt; her name was found on a ring he wore. She had been waiting for him.

The Iron Brigade went into Herbst Woods and broke Archer's Confederate brigade -- the attack Reynolds had set in motion with his life. But Reynolds was gone, and the Army of the Potomac would fight the next two days without the man who might have made all the difference."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "John F. Reynolds commanded the I Corps and, under Meade's orders, the left wing of the army (the I, III and XI Corps). Meade's report records that Reynolds was directed to occupy Gettysburg and that, on reaching it, he found Buford's cavalry warmly engaged with the enemy. He sent orders for the XI Corps to advance as promptly as possible and put the Iron Brigade into the woods west of McPherson's Ridge.

He was shot near the eastern edge of the woods as the Iron Brigade went in. Doubleday, close by, learned 'with deep sorrow' that 'our brave and lamented commander, Major-General Reynolds, had just been shot, and was no more', and puts it at about 10:15 a.m.; Howard's reports of the same day say 11:15, and his later report 11:30, which is when Howard was told. The cause is unsettled: Heth believed one of the first shells from Pegram's guns struck him, and the usual account names a sharpshooter.

Doubleday took the I Corps and Howard the field when he arrived. Reynolds, whose decision to fight west of the town had brought the army into the battle, was dead within the first hour of the infantry fight."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/1 p.114 (Meade), p.245 (Doubleday: "about 10.15 a. m."), p.696 (Howard 11.15), p.702, p.727 (11.30); OR 27/2 p.637 (Heth); ledger WSD-14. The offer of army command was Lincoln's, not Meade's, and is dropped

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Within minutes of Reynolds's death, the Iron Brigade's charge through Herbst Woods captured Confederate General James Archer -- the first Confederate general officer taken prisoner since Lee assumed command of the army. Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin personally seized Archer as he tried to escape across Willoughby Run."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "The Iron Brigade's counterattack drove Archer's brigade back across the Willoughby Run and captured Brigadier General James J. Archer, brought in by Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin, who was killed later in the day. Doubleday reported nearly 1,000 prisoners from Archer's brigade; Heth said Archer was lost with some 60 or 70 of his men."
patches.note: unsupported-claim: OR 27/1 p.245 (Doubleday), p.274 (2nd Wisconsin); OR 27/2 p.638 (Heth)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The Iron Brigade swept through Herbst Woods like a tide. Archer's Tennessee and Alabama brigade had advanced confidently that morning -- they expected Pennsylvania militia, not the best infantry in the Army of the Potomac.

The black hats changed everything. A Confederate soldier who recognized them shouted a warning: 'That's no militia -- that's the Army of the Potomac!' But it was too late.

The Iron Brigade's left regiments -- the 2nd and 7th Wisconsin -- swept south of the Chambersburg Pike and curled around Archer's right flank. Archer's brigade, caught in the flank, broke. Men streamed back toward Willoughby Run, some plunging into the water to escape.

Brigadier General James J. Archer was trying to cross the run when Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin grabbed him by the collar.

Archer was a small, sick man -- he had been ill for weeks and had no business commanding a brigade in the field. He looked up at the private holding him and said simply that he would not be taken.

Maloney held on.

Archer was brought to Doubleday, who had just assumed command after Reynolds's death. The two men knew each other from before the war. Doubleday extended his hand and said cheerfully, 'Good morning, Archer! How are you? I am glad to see you!'

Archer refused to shake hands. 'Well, I am not glad to see YOU by a damn sight, Doubleday.'

He was the first Confederate general officer captured since Lee had taken command of the Army of Northern Virginia. He would spend the rest of the campaign in a Union prison."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Meredith's brigade formed, right to left, the 2nd Wisconsin, 7th Wisconsin, 19th Indiana and 24th Michigan. Doubleday writes that it 'deployed en echelon without a moment's hesitation, charged with the utmost steadiness and fury, hurled the enemy back into the run', led by the 2nd Wisconsin in line.

'To it also belongs the honor of capturing General Archer himself. He was brought in by Private Patrick Maloney, of Company G. It is to be lamented that this brave Irishman was subsequently killed in the action.' The 2nd Wisconsin's own report says Archer was taken by Maloney 'and brought to me, to whom he surrendered his sword'.

The prisoner count is disputed. Doubleday says nearly 1,000, all from Archer's brigade; Heth says Archer fell into the enemy's hands 'together with some 60 or 70 of his men'. A much-told exchange between Archer and Doubleday, who had known each other before the war, comes from later accounts, not from the reports. By Doubleday's order the Iron Brigade was then withdrawn to the east side of the run and re-formed on the high ground."
patches.note: unsupported-claim: OR 27/1 p.245 (Doubleday), p.274 (2nd Wisconsin); OR 27/2 p.638 (Heth)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Colonel Rufus Dawes led the 6th Wisconsin in a desperate charge across the Chambersburg Pike and into the unfinished Railroad Cut, where Davis's Confederate brigade had taken cover. The cut proved a trap -- too deep to escape under fire. The 6th Wisconsin captured 232 men in one of the most decisive small-unit actions of the battle."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Lieutenant Colonel Rufus Dawes's 6th Wisconsin, with the 95th New York and the 14th Brooklyn, charged Davis's Confederates in the unfinished Railroad Cut north of the Chambersburg Pike. The men in the cut threw down their arms; the 6th Wisconsin sent to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men and took the 2nd Mississippi's flag."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.246 (Doubleday), p.275-276 (Dawes: "7 officers and about 225 men"; Blair; Waller; 160)

patches.find:
"full_script": "Rufus Dawes had been a schoolteacher before the war. On the morning of July 1, 1863, he was commanding the 6th Wisconsin -- the largest regiment in the Iron Brigade -- and watching Davis's Confederate brigade sweep north past his position toward the unfinished railroad cut.

Dawes received orders to charge. He turned to his men.

'Six Wisconsin, advance!' The regiment stepped off at the double-quick, moving north across the Chambersburg Pike. The 14th Brooklyn -- red-legged Zouaves -- joined on their left. The 95th New York came with them.

Davis's men had ducked into the railroad cut for cover. It seemed perfect -- a ready-made trench running east-west. What Davis had not understood was that the western portion of the cut was fifteen feet deep. His men were trapped in a ditch.

Dawes's regiment hit the cut at a run. The fighting was vicious -- men stabbed each other with bayonets across a gap of feet, grappled over regimental flags, fired at point-blank range. But the Confederates could not climb the sheer walls under fire.

Dawes reached the middle of the cut and shouted across to the Confederate officer opposite him: 'Where is the colonel of this regiment?'

'Who are you?' the officer called back.

'I am Colonel Dawes of the 6th Wisconsin. I demand the immediate and unconditional surrender of this regiment!'

There was a pause. Then the Confederate flag dipped, and men began throwing down their arms.

Dawes captured 232 prisoners -- nearly a full regiment -- in a single charge. The regimental flag of the 2nd Mississippi was taken. Davis's brigade had been broken for the second time in a morning."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Doubleday had held the 6th Wisconsin out of the Iron Brigade as a reserve. When Davis's Mississippians and North Carolinians drove back Cutler's right and threatened the rear of the brigade fighting in the woods, he sent it against their flank. Dawes brought it up at the double-quick, checked the enemy with a fire by file at about 40 rods, and found them taking refuge in the unfinished railroad cut. The 95th New York and the 14th Brooklyn joined on his left.

Dawes ordered the charge. 'When our line reached the edge of the cut, the rebels began throwing down their arms in token of surrender.' Major John A. Blair surrendered the 2nd Mississippi; Major Hauser reports sending to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men. The regiment's battle flag was taken by Corporal F. Asbury Waller. The 6th Wisconsin lost not less than 160 men killed or wounded.

Doubleday says two regiments of Davis's brigade were taken with their flags, the 147th New York was released and a gun of Hall's battery recovered, all in less than half an hour and before Howard arrived. Dawes's well-known exchange with a Confederate officer ('Where is the colonel of this regiment?') is from his memoir of 1890, not from his report."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.246 (Doubleday), p.275-276 (Dawes: "7 officers and about 225 men"; Blair; Waller; 160)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Brigadier General Alfred Iverson sent his North Carolina brigade forward without skirmishers, without reconnaissance, and apparently without personally leading the charge. His men advanced in perfect alignment directly toward a stone wall behind which Baxter's Union brigade lay waiting. In minutes, approximately 500 of Iverson's 1,470 men were shot down in rows. The shallow graves of his men are visible as depressions in the ground at Oak Ridge to this day."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Iverson's North Carolina brigade attacked the stone wall on Oak Ridge held by Robinson's division, was struck by musketry from behind it, and lost heavily; Rodes wrote that its dead 'lay in a distinctly marked line of battle'. The Confederate return prints 820 casualties for the brigade, though its own rows add to 763."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.553-554 (Rodes), p.444 (Ewell), p.342 page image (return)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The field north of Gettysburg was quiet when Iverson's four North Carolina regiments stepped off. They moved in perfect alignment -- a textbook advance that would have drawn admiration on a parade ground. No skirmishers preceded them. No one had scouted the stone wall ahead.

Behind that wall, Baxter's Union brigade lay flat in the grass, waiting. The 12th Massachusetts, 83rd New York, 97th New York, 88th Pennsylvania, 90th Pennsylvania -- all pressed close to the ground, rifles ready.

Iverson's men had covered perhaps half the distance when Baxter's soldiers rose up behind the wall and fired.

The volley came simultaneously along a front of several hundred yards. Iverson's regiments were struck in the flank -- the wall ran parallel to their line of advance. Men fell in rows exactly as they had been marching, in perfect military alignment, because there had been no time to break formation before the fire swept through them.

About 500 men fell in the first minutes. Not wounded -- fell, shot, lying in the grass in the same lines they had been marching in.

Iverson, watching from behind, reportedly believed his men had surrendered. He sent word to Rodes that his brigade had thrown up the white flag in dishonor. It was not true. His men were not surrendering. They were dying.

When Union soldiers advanced after the battle to bury the dead, they found the bodies lying in such perfect order that little digging was needed. They buried them where they fell, in shallow trenches that followed the line of the advance.

The slight depressions of those graves are visible at Oak Ridge today.

Iverson was relieved of command shortly after the battle. He was never given another brigade."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Rodes sent Iverson's brigade forward and gave O'Neal the order to attack at the same moment. O'Neal's brigade went in with only three of its regiments, in confusion and not in the direction Rodes had ordered, and was quickly repulsed; Rodes says O'Neal, instead of leading it, had stayed with the 5th Alabama, which Rodes himself had held back.

Iverson's brigade, Rodes reports, 'attacked handsomely, but suffered very heavily from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge'. With O'Neal repulsed, Iverson's left was exposed: 'His men fought and died like heroes. His dead lay in a distinctly marked line of battle. His left was overpowered, and many of his men, being surrounded, were captured.'

Ewell adds that Iverson wrongly sent word to Rodes that one of his regiments had raised the white flag and gone over to the enemy. The Confederate return of casualties prints 130 killed, 328 wounded, 308 captured or missing and 820 in all for the brigade; its regimental rows add to 455 killed and wounded and 308 missing or captured, 763, so the table disagrees with itself. Iverson's strength is not given in the reports read."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.553-554 (Rodes), p.444 (Ewell), p.342 page image (return)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "When Gordon's Confederate brigade swept over Barlow's Knoll, General Francis Barlow was shot and left for dead among his fallen men. Confederate General John Gordon rode to the dying Union general, gave him water, tried to comfort him, and promised to find his wife. The two men met again after the war and became friends -- one of the most remarkable reconciliation stories of the conflict."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Gordon's brigade broke Barlow's division on the knoll north of Gettysburg and Barlow, severely wounded, was captured. The story that Gordon gave him water, promised to tell his wife, and years later met him as a friend comes from Gordon's own later account; some of its details have been questioned, and none is in the Official Records."
patches.note: unsupported-claim: OR 27/2 p.445, p.469 (Ewell), p.493 (Gordon); OR 27/1 p.729 (Schurz)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The charge of Gordon's Georgia brigade had swept everything before it. When it was over, when the Union line on Barlow's Knoll had collapsed and the Confederates were pursuing the broken XI Corps south toward Gettysburg, John Gordon rode over the ground his men had taken.

He found a Union general lying among the dead, shot through the body and left behind in the rout. The man was barely conscious.

Gordon dismounted. He raised the officer's head, gave him water from his own canteen, tried to make him comfortable. He asked if there was anything he could do.

The dying man -- it was General Francis Barlow, commanding the First Division of the XI Corps -- said he did not expect to live. He asked Gordon, if it were possible, to find his wife and tell her where he had fallen.

Gordon promised. He had the general moved to a shaded spot and left a Confederate soldier to care for him. Then he rejoined the pursuit.

Barlow did not die. Against all expectation, he recovered -- slowly, painfully -- and returned to command. He served through the rest of the war. He became one of the best Union division commanders at the Overland Campaign.

After the war, Gordon heard a rumor that Barlow had died. Barlow heard a rumor that Gordon had died. They never sought each other out.

Years later, at a dinner party in Washington, two men were introduced and recognized each other simultaneously.

It was Gordon. It was Barlow.

They had both assumed the other was dead. They became friends. Gordon told the story many times in his postwar lectures -- the enemy officer he had cared for on the field at Gettysburg, the man he had thought was dying, sitting across a dinner table from him in the nation's capital.

'We became fast friends,' Gordon wrote, 'and so we shall remain while we both live.'"
patches.repl: "full_script": "Ewell reports that Early ordered Gordon's brigade in on the left of Doles's, and that after an obstinate contest it 'broke Barlow's division, captured General Barlow, and drove the whole back on a second line'. Schurz writes that Barlow, who 'had been directing the movements of his troops with the most praiseworthy coolness and intrepidity', was severely wounded and carried off, and that the division passed to General Ames.\n\nGordon told another story many times after the war: that he found the wounded Barlow on the field, gave him water, promised to tell his wife where he lay, and that the two men met years later, each believing the other dead, and became friends. That account is Gordon's; some of its details have been questioned, and neither the reports nor the Official Records contain it."
patches.note: unsupported-claim: OR 27/2 p.445, p.469 (Ewell), p.493 (Gordon); OR 27/1 p.729 (Schurz)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Against direct orders, General Daniel Sickles advanced his entire III Corps nearly a mile forward from its assigned position on Cemetery Ridge to the Peach Orchard on the Emmitsburg Road. The move created a dangerously exposed salient. When Longstreet's assault struck it that afternoon, the salient collapsed in catastrophe -- but Sickles would spend the rest of his long life arguing he had been right."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "On July 2 Sickles's III Corps advanced from the line of Cemetery Ridge toward the Emmitsburg road, making a salient at the Peach Orchard. Meade's report says Sickles, 'not fully apprehending the instructions', was advancing half a mile to three-quarters of a mile in front of the Second Corps line when Meade found him about 3 p.m.; whether the move was authorized and when it began are disputed."
patches.note: contested-fact: OR 27/1 p.115-116 (Meade); time-facts R050

patches.find:
"full_script": "Daniel Sickles was a politician, a killer, and -- in his own estimation -- a military genius. He had shot his wife's lover on the steps of the White House and been acquitted by reason of temporary insanity -- the first successful use of that defense in American legal history. He had wangled a general's commission despite no military training whatsoever. He had survived every disaster through audacity, charm, and a complete inability to recognize that he might be wrong.

On the morning of July 2, 1863, he stared at the ground his corps had been assigned and decided it was unsuitable. The Peach Orchard, a quarter-mile to the west along the Emmitsburg Road, sat on slightly higher ground. In Sickles's judgment, the Peach Orchard was the position he should hold.

He did not ask Meade. He did not request permission. He did not inform his commander.

Around 3:00 in the afternoon, Sickles moved his entire corps -- 10,000 men and dozens of artillery pieces -- forward to the Emmitsburg Road.

Meade discovered the movement and rode south in fury. He found Sickles sitting on horseback in the new line and demanded an explanation. Sickles began to explain. Meade interrupted: the position was untenable. The line was too long. The flanks were exposed. The corps should go back.

At that moment, Longstreet's guns opened fire.

'I will withdraw if you order it,' Sickles said.

'I do order it,' Meade replied. 'But the enemy will not allow you to.'

He was right. Within the hour, the Peach Orchard would become the most violent piece of ground on the continent.

Sickles lost his right leg to an artillery shell that afternoon. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar -- a gesture for his men. He spent the rest of his life, another fifty years, insisting that his unauthorized advance had saved the Army of the Potomac by drawing Confederate attention away from Little Round Top. Most historians disagree. But Sickles never changed his story."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Meade's report says the II and III Corps were directed to occupy the continuation of Cemetery Ridge on the left of the XI Corps. About 3 p.m. he rode to the extreme left to await the V Corps and 'found that Major-General Sickles, commanding the Third Corps, not fully apprehending the instructions in regard to the position to be occupied, had advanced, or rather was in the act of advancing, his corps some half a mile or three-quarters of a mile in front of the line of the Second Corps'.

Meade writes that he was explaining to Sickles that he was too far in advance, and discussing the propriety of withdrawing, when the enemy opened with several batteries in his front and on his flank and brought up columns of infantry in a vigorous assault. The hour of the advance is itself disputed: accounts put it anywhere from noon to about 3:30 p.m.

The III Corps fought hard in its advanced line; Sickles was wounded early in the action and Birney took the corps, and it was forced back to the line originally designed. Sickles maintained for the rest of his life that the advance had been right. Words attributed to him and to Meade at this meeting come from later testimony, not from the reports."
patches.note: contested-fact: OR 27/1 p.115-116 (Meade); time-facts R050

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Colonel Hiram Berdan led his regiment of green-uniformed sharpshooters into Pitzer's Woods on a reconnaissance ordered by Sickles. They found Wilcox's Confederate infantry already positioned there -- confirming Confederate activity on Seminary Ridge south of town. The reconnaissance gave Sickles his justification for advancing to the Peach Orchard."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "About 11 a.m. on July 2 Birney ordered Colonel Berdan to feel the enemy beyond the Union left. Berdan took 100 men of the 1st U.S. Sharpshooters, with the 3rd Maine in support, down the Emmitsburg road, ran into Confederate columns changing direction in the woods beyond, attacked them, and withdrew; he reported to Birney about 2 p.m."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/1 p.515 (Berdan)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The sharpshooters of Berdan's regiment were the best shots in the Union Army. Recruited for their marksmanship, equipped with Sharps repeating rifles, dressed in green uniforms that made them harder to see in the woods -- they were an elite within an army that still largely fought in shoulder-to-shoulder lines.

On the morning of July 2, Sickles was worried about his left. Buford's cavalry had departed. There was open ground stretching south and west, and nobody knew what was on the other side of Pitzer's Woods on Seminary Ridge.

Sickles ordered Berdan to find out.

The 1st US Sharpshooters moved into the woods in skirmish order -- open files, each man moving independently, using cover. No solid lines. No drumbeats. Just green-coated men filtering into the dark trees.

They found Wilcox's Alabama brigade.

The firefight was sharp and brief. The sharpshooters fell back with their information: there were Confederate infantry on Seminary Ridge, south of town, already in position. Longstreet's corps was there.

Berdan returned with his report. Sickles had what he needed.

Whether the reconnaissance actually showed what Sickles claimed it showed -- a Confederate flanking movement about to swing around his left -- is a matter historians still debate. What is certain is that Sickles used it as justification for advancing his entire corps to the Emmitsburg Road without orders. Whether Berdan's intelligence warranted that response, and whether the advance saved or nearly destroyed the Army of the Potomac, has been argued for 160 years."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Berdan commanded the First and Second Regiments of Sharpshooters. His report says that about 7:30 a.m. he sent forward a detachment of 100 men who held the crest beyond the Emmitsburg road all day, and that about 11 a.m. Birney ordered another detachment of 100 sharpshooters, with the Third Maine as support, to feel the enemy and discover his movements.

'I moved down the Emmitsburg road some distance beyond our extreme left and deployed the sharpshooters in a line running nearly east and west ... We soon came upon the enemy, and drove them sufficiently to discover three columns in motion in rear of the woods, changing direction, as it were, by the right flank.' The Union force attacked on the flank and threw the Confederates into confusion; they rallied and attacked in turn, and Berdan withdrew under cover of the woods, 'having accomplished the object of the reconnaissance', and reported about 2 o'clock to Birney.

Which Confederate brigade he met is not named in his report. How much weight the reconnaissance gave to Sickles's later decision to advance is disputed."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/1 p.515 (Berdan)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "With Little Round Top undefended and Confederate infantry racing to take it, General Warren intercepted Vincent's brigade on the march and redirected it up the hill. Vincent placed his regiments on the slope just minutes before Law's Confederates arrived. Colonel Strong Vincent was mortally wounded holding the position he had seized -- he died a brigadier general, his promotion arriving while he lay dying."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "On July 2 Colonel Strong Vincent's brigade of the V Corps climbed Little Round Top and was posted on its southern slope, with the 20th Maine on the extreme left, minutes before the Confederate attack; Sykes's report says the troops were posted under Warren's direction. Vincent was mortally wounded in the fight and Colonel Rice took the brigade."
patches.note: contested-fact: OR 27/1 p.623 (Chamberlain), p.593 (Sykes)

patches.find:
"full_script": "Gouverneur Warren stood on the summit of Little Round Top and understood in an instant what was about to happen.

The hill was empty. Below and to the south, through his field glasses, he could see the glint of sunlight on rifle barrels and bayonets -- Law's Confederate division moving through the trees at the base of Big Round Top, angling toward the rocky slope where Warren stood alone.

If the Confederates took Little Round Top, their artillery would command the entire Union line on Cemetery Ridge from the south. The army would have to retreat or be destroyed. Warren sent aides galloping in every direction: get troops, any troops, get them up this hill now.

The first aide found Colonel Strong Vincent commanding his brigade on the road below. Vincent did not wait for formal orders -- he did not have time for formal orders. 'I will take the responsibility of taking my brigade there,' he told the aide, and immediately led his four regiments up the rocky face of Little Round Top.

Vincent placed his regiments himself, walking the ground with quick precision: 16th Michigan on the right, 44th New York in the center, 83rd Pennsylvania center-left, 20th Maine on the extreme left. He was explicit about the left: 'This is the left of the Union line. You must hold this ground at all costs.'

He said this to Colonel Joshua Chamberlain of the 20th Maine.

Within minutes of the last regiment reaching its position, Confederate infantry appeared at the base of the slope.

Vincent was shot through the groin late in the afternoon while trying to rally the 16th Michigan. His men carried him from the field. He lingered for five days. On July 7, as he was dying, word came that he had been promoted to brigadier general. Those around him told him the news. He smiled.

'Did I not tell you that I would be a general officer before the battle was over?' he said.

He died that afternoon."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Chamberlain's report says that his brigade, near 4 p.m., hurried toward a cannonade on the left, and that when it reached a wood 'we received from Colonel Vincent, commanding the brigade, orders to move to the left at the double-quick' to gain the rugged spur known as Little Round Top. 'Passing to the southern slope ... Colonel Vincent indicated to me the ground my regiment was to occupy, informing me that this was the extreme left of our general line, and that a desperate attack was expected in order to turn that position, concluding by telling me I was to "hold that ground at all hazards." This was the last word I heard from him.'

The brigade's line, from left to right, was the 20th Maine, 83rd Pennsylvania, 44th New York and 16th Michigan. Sykes writes that Vincent's brigade 'had seized the rocky height, closely followed by Weed's brigade' and that they 'were posted under the direction of General Warren'. Whether Warren, Meade's chief engineer, found the hill held only by a signal station and sent for troops, or Vincent acted on his own initiative, is told differently in later accounts.

Vincent and Weed fell in the fighting; Sykes names Vincent, Weed and Hazlett as 'chiefs lamented throughout the corps and army' who 'sealed with their lives the spot intrusted to their keeping'. Rice took the brigade."
patches.note: contested-fact: OR 27/1 p.623 (Chamberlain), p.593 (Sykes)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "After repulsing five Confederate assaults with nearly empty cartridge boxes, Colonel Joshua Chamberlain ordered the 20th Maine to fix bayonets and charge downhill. The attack swept the 15th Alabama from the slope and captured nearly 400 prisoners. It was the most celebrated regimental action of the battle -- and possibly of the entire war."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "At a crisis on the left of Little Round Top Colonel Chamberlain ordered the 20th Maine to the bayonet. The regiment swept down the hill and the Confederate front line threw down its arms. Chamberlain reported 400 prisoners, mainly from the 15th and 47th Alabama with some of the 4th and 5th Texas, and 150 of the enemy killed and wounded in front of his position; the hour of the charge is disputed."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.623-624 (Chamberlain); time-facts R066; the Medal of Honor date (1893) is well documented and left as before

patches.find:
"full_script": "Joshua Chamberlain had been a professor of rhetoric at Bowdoin College before the war. He had taught himself tactics by reading military manuals at night. On the afternoon of July 2, 1863, he had already repulsed five Confederate assaults on the left flank of the entire Union Army.

His regiment was nearly out of ammunition.

The 15th Alabama, under Colonel William Oates, had been trying to turn the 20th Maine's refused left flank for nearly an hour. Each time, Chamberlain's men had stopped them. But the cartridge boxes were almost empty. The men were telling their officers they had nothing left to fire.

Oates was preparing another charge.

Chamberlain had two choices: retreat, or attack. Retreat was unacceptable -- his orders were to hold at all costs. Attack with empty rifles seemed suicidal. But Chamberlain understood something Oates did not: the Confederates below were as exhausted as the men above. The 15th Alabama had marched twenty-five miles that day before climbing and assaulting the hill. If he could shock them with an unexpected counter-charge, they might break before they understood what was happening.

'Fix bayonets,' Chamberlain ordered.

The command passed down the line. The 20th Maine -- fewer than 200 men still standing in the ranks -- fixed bayonets.

'Charge!'

The regiment swept downhill in a right-wheel motion, pivoting around the center and sweeping south and west. Chamberlain led from the front, a pistol in one hand and a saber in the other.

Oates's men, climbing uphill toward what they expected to be a final assault on a shattered regiment, were instead hit by a wall of screaming men coming downhill at them.

The 15th Alabama broke.

The 20th Maine captured nearly 400 prisoners. Chamberlain was slightly wounded -- twice. He would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions on Little Round Top, presented thirty years after the battle. At the war's end, Ulysses Grant chose Chamberlain to receive the formal Confederate surrender at Appomattox."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Chamberlain's regiment stood on the extreme left of the Union line. He saw 'a considerable body of the enemy moving by the flank in rear of their line engaged' and stretched his regiment to the left, taking intervals and 'refusing' the left wing so that it stood nearly at right angles to the right, 'thus occupying about twice the extent of our ordinary front'. The flanking column 'burst upon my left'; the fight went on at close range, with the line withering and ammunition running low.

'It was imperative to strike before we were struck by this overwhelming force in a hand-to-hand fight, which we could not probably have withstood or survived. At that crisis, I ordered the bayonet. The word was enough. It ran like fire along the line, from man to man, and rose into a shout, with which they sprang forward upon the enemy, now not 30 yards away. The effect was surprising; many of the enemy's first line threw down their arms and surrendered.'

'Four hundred prisoners, including two field and several line officers, were sent to the rear', he wrote, mainly from the 15th and 47th Alabama with some of the 4th and 5th Texas, and 150 of the enemy were found killed and wounded in front. The hour is disputed: accounts range from about 5:10 to after 7 p.m. Chamberlain received the Medal of Honor in 1893."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.623-624 (Chamberlain); time-facts R066; the Medal of Honor date (1893) is well documented and left as before

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Captain John Bigelow's 9th Massachusetts Battery was ordered to hold the Trostle Farm without infantry support -- to buy time for McGilvery to form the artillery line that would stop the Confederate breakthrough. The battery fought its withdrawal by prolonge, losing men and guns but accomplishing its mission. A cannonball through the barn wall is still visible today."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "The 9th Massachusetts Battery (six 12-pounder Napoleons), supporting the III Corps, covered the withdrawal of the batteries on its right and then retired by prolonge, firing as it went, to a position near two stone walls at the Trostle farm, which it was ordered to hold at all hazards without infantry support. It lost 8 killed, 17 wounded and 2 prisoners, and four of its guns were left in the field and recovered the same day, while McGilvery formed a line of guns behind it."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/1 p.886 (Milton: prolonge, 300 yards, "hold at all hazards", four pieces silenced and recovered, casualties, 45 horses); p.685 (a Napoleon recaptured)

patches.find:
"full_script": "Lieutenant Colonel McGilvery rode up to Captain John Bigelow at a gallop.

'I must have time,' McGilvery said. 'You must stay here and hold at any cost until I can form a new line.'

Bigelow looked around. His battery -- six Napoleon guns, nine horses each -- was already under fire from Barksdale's Mississippi infantry advancing from the Peach Orchard. There was no infantry support anywhere nearby. McGilvery was asking him to hold a position unsupported against a brigade of Confederate infantry.

'How long?' Bigelow asked.

'As long as you can,' McGilvery said, and rode away.

Bigelow ordered his battery to hook their guns to prolonges -- long ropes that allowed artillerymen to move the guns while still firing -- and begin a fighting withdrawal through the Trostle Farm lane.

What followed was one of the most desperate artillery actions of the war. The 9th Massachusetts fired as they retreated, horses falling, men dropping at the guns. Bigelow was wounded. The battery lost one gun stuck in a stone wall as Confederate infantry closed in from three sides. The last section fired canister into advancing Mississippians from a range of fifty yards.

Bigelow lost 28 men and one gun. He bought McGilvery the twenty minutes he needed.

When Confederate infantry finally overran the Trostle Farm, they found it abandoned. McGilvery's Plum Run Line was formed and waiting.

The cannonball hole in the Trostle Farm barn wall -- a Confederate artillery round that missed Bigelow's withdrawing battery -- is still visible today. It is one of the most photographed details on the Gettysburg battlefield."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Lieutenant Milton, who took the battery when Bigelow was wounded, reports that the battery went into line about 4 p.m. on the extreme left, beside the batteries of the Third Corps, and fired slowly for an hour at the enemy's batteries about 1,600 yards in front. When the Third Corps fell back, 'leaving us without support', and the Confederate infantry advanced in two lines across its front, the battery covered the withdrawal of the batteries on its right and, 'prolonges being fixed, and firing at skirmishers on our left and the approaching line of battle on our right, we retired 300 yards' to a position where two stone walls met at an obtuse angle.

'This position, without infantry support and under an enfilading artillery fire, we were ordered to hold at all hazards. The rebel line of battle could not be checked, although its center was badly broken by our canister fire. Its flanks closing in on either side of us, obtained a cross-fire, which silenced the four pieces on my right, and prevented their withdrawal from loss of officers, men, and horses.' Milton got a section away and, under McGilvery's orders, withdrew a mile and a half to the rear, reaching park at 9 p.m.; 'our four guns were recovered the same day.'

The battery lost 1 officer, 1 sergeant and 6 men killed, 2 officers, 6 non-commissioned officers and 9 men wounded, 2 taken prisoners, 45 horses killed and 15 wounded. The words attributed to McGilvery and Bigelow in later retellings, and the link between this fight and the shell hole in the Trostle barn, are tradition, not in the report."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/1 p.886 (Milton: prolonge, 300 yards, "hold at all hazards", four pieces silenced and recovered, casualties, 45 horses); p.685 (a Napoleon recaptured)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "With Cemetery Ridge open and Wilcox's Confederate brigade advancing toward the gap, General Hancock turned to the only regiment near at hand -- 262 men of the 1st Minnesota. He ordered them to charge an entire Confederate brigade to buy five minutes for reinforcements to arrive. They did it. 224 of 262 men fell. The regiment suffered the highest casualty rate of any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "With Confederate columns reaching the gap in the line on July 2, Hancock ordered Colonel Colvill's 1st Minnesota to take the enemy's colors, wanting to gain time until reinforcements came up. The regiment charged and drove the enemy back. Fox counts 262 engaged and 224 casualties, nearly all in this fight, none missing; 215 were killed or wounded on July 2 itself, the highest percentage of any Union regiment in a single battle in his tables."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/1 p.371 (Hancock); Fox p.26 (account; 262 men; 50 killed, 174 wounded, 224; none missing), p.36 (215 on July 2; 82.0), p.402; ledger WSD-12

patches.find:
"full_script": "Winfield Scott Hancock had been riding hard along Cemetery Ridge for twenty minutes, trying to hold together a line that was dissolving in front of him. The III Corps was gone -- shattered, streaming back from the Peach Orchard and the Wheatfield. The gap in the Union center was real and it was widening.

Across the fields, Cadmus Wilcox's Alabama brigade was advancing at the double-quick toward that gap. If they reached Cemetery Ridge, the Union line would be cut in two.

Hancock turned in his saddle. The only regiment near at hand was the 1st Minnesota -- 262 officers and men under Colonel William Colvill.

'My God, are these all the men we have here?' Hancock said.

Then he ordered them forward.

Colvill understood what the order meant. He turned to his regiment: 'Forward, double-quick!'

The 262 men of the 1st Minnesota -- a state with fewer than 200,000 people -- charged into Wilcox's entire brigade.

The fighting was savage and brief. The regiment drove into the Confederate line with bayonets and clubbed rifles, and for a few minutes the Confederate advance actually stopped. The Alabamians had not expected this. They had not expected anything to be there at all.

But 262 men cannot hold long against 1,700. The 1st Minnesota was shredded. Colvill went down, shot in three places. The regimental commander, the lieutenant colonel, the major -- all hit. Companies were reduced to handfuls. The regiment fell back toward Cemetery Ridge.

But they had bought the five minutes Hancock needed. Reinforcements arrived and closed the gap.

Of 262 men who charged, 224 were casualties -- 85.5%. It remains the highest casualty rate suffered by any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war.

The survivors -- 38 men -- formed in line the next morning and were ordered to hold the same ground. They did."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Fox tells it this way. While Hancock was 'patching' up a second line he saw a column of the enemy, Willcox's brigade, emerge from a clump of trees near an unprotected part of his line. The First Minnesota, alone and unsupported, was near by, and Hancock, wishing to gain time until reinforcements could be brought up, rode to Colonel Colvill and ordered him to take the enemy's colors. A desperate fight followed in which the enemy was forced back, leaving their colors with the First Minnesota.

Hancock's own report says the regiment 'charged the rebel regiment in handsome style, capturing its colors, and driving it back in disorder', and that in its attack and its later advance it 'lost three-fourths of the officers and men engaged'. Hancock is reported to have said afterward that he saw he must gain five minutes' time.

The regiment took 262 officers and men in; Fox counts 50 killed and 174 wounded, 224 casualties in all, with none missing. His table puts the loss on July 2 at 215 of 262, 82.0 percent, and ranks it highest among Union regiments in a single battle; the 224 includes the next day. Hancock's exact words to Colvill, and the regimental count of survivors the next morning, vary between accounts."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/1 p.371 (Hancock); Fox p.26 (account; 262 men; 50 killed, 174 wounded, 224; none missing), p.36 (215 on July 2; 82.0), p.402; ledger WSD-12

patches.find: "panel_summary": "When the XII Corps was stripped from Culp's Hill to reinforce Cemetery Ridge, only George Greene's New York brigade remained -- 1,424 men to hold the position against Johnson's entire Confederate division of 6,500. Greene extended his line impossibly thin and held for three hours. It was one of the finest defensive performances of the entire war."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "When most of the XII Corps was sent to the left on July 2, Greene's brigade of five New York regiments (74 officers and 1,350 men by Geary's count, 1,424 in all) held the entrenched Culp's Hill alone against Johnson's division, which attacked about two hours after the opening on the right; Greene was reinforced during the evening by detachments from the I and XI Corps."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.121 (Slocum), p.833 (Geary), p.858 (Greene); OR 27/2 p.319 (Lee)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The orders came at dusk: Slocum was pulling the XII Corps south to reinforce the crumbling Union left. The brigades would move -- all of them. All except Greene's.

Brigadier General George Greene was sixty-two years old, the oldest brigade commander at Gettysburg. He was a West Point engineer who had spent his career building aqueducts and railroads. His five New York regiments -- 1,424 men -- were to hold Culp's Hill while the rest of the corps departed.

Greene looked at his line. His five regiments normally occupied perhaps 600 yards of front. The entire XII Corps position was more than 1,300 yards. He was being asked to hold more than double his normal front -- with the same number of men -- against Johnson's Confederate division of 6,500.

Greene had spent his career as an engineer. He understood defensive works. During the afternoon, while the army was fighting in the south, he had ordered his men to build breastworks -- proper log-and-earth fortifications, not just scratched rifle pits. His officers had thought it excessive. Now those breastworks would save his command.

Greene extended his line by thinning it beyond any conventional military standard. A man here, a man there, a twenty-foot gap between. The works did the work that bodies could not.

Johnson's division attacked in waves. The Stonewall Brigade, Jones's brigade, Nicholls's brigade -- all came up the dark hill into the abatis and the fire from Greene's thin line.

Greene held.

For three hours, 1,424 men held Culp's Hill against 6,500. Steuart's brigade, on the Confederate left, found the empty XII Corps works and occupied them -- but they could not advance past Greene's position. The upper hill stayed Union.

When the XII Corps returned in the darkness, they found Greene still holding, his line still unbroken. He had lost 303 men. He had saved the Union right flank."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Slocum reports that the troops left on the extreme right were Greene's brigade of the Second Division, holding the left of the XII Corps, now the extreme right of the army. The enemy, seeing the withdrawal, advanced and attacked Greene, who made 'a gallant defense' and was 'soon re-enforced by portions of the First and Eleventh Corps', and repulsed all efforts to dislodge him.

Geary's statement of numbers taken into the engagement gives Greene's brigade 74 officers and 1,350 men. Greene himself counts his own brigade 1,350 with 355 sent from the First Corps, 400 from the Eleventh and part of Candy's brigade, 3,105 in all, of whom he says not more than 1,300 were in the line. Lee says Johnson attacked about two hours after Longstreet's batteries opened, with three brigades, the fourth being detained by a demonstration on his left, and that Steuart's brigade carried part of the works.

After dark, when the detachments returned from the left, it was found that the enemy occupied part of the XII Corps' line of breastworks; Williams arranged to retake them at daylight. The Confederate strength engaged is not given in the reports read here."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.121 (Slocum), p.833 (Geary), p.858 (Greene); OR 27/2 p.319 (Lee)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "At dusk on July 2, Hays's Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade stormed Cemetery Hill in near-darkness. They reached the crest, seized Union artillery, and held it briefly -- the closest any Confederate force came to breaking the Union center. Colonel Avery was mortally wounded on the slope, writing his last message in his own blood."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "At dusk on July 2 Hays's Louisiana brigade and Hoke's North Carolina brigade, under Colonel Avery, charged Cemetery Hill from the town. Lee's report says they drove two lines from the fences, forced their way into the works on the crest and seized several pieces of artillery, but a heavy force advanced against their unsupported right and they were compelled to retire, bringing out about 100 prisoners and four stand of colors."
patches.note: contradiction: OR 27/2 p.319 (Lee); the note is tradition and labelled

patches.find:
"full_script": "The Louisiana Tigers had a reputation. In an army of hard men they were considered especially dangerous -- New Orleans toughs, dock workers, immigrants, men with nothing to lose. Their officers sometimes controlled them with threats of summary execution. On the battlefield, they were formidable.

At dusk on July 2, Hays's five Louisiana regiments and Avery's three North Carolina regiments stepped off from the town of Gettysburg and began climbing Cemetery Hill.

The timing was not accidental. The Union artillery on the hill could not depress their guns enough to fire directly at men climbing the steep slope below them. The light was failing. The Confederate attack would have to be met with musketry alone.

Hays's men swept up the hill with a ferocity that overwhelmed the XI Corps units defending the lower slope. They reached the crest. They seized the Union guns. For a few minutes -- perhaps ten, perhaps fifteen -- Louisiana and North Carolina men stood on the summit of Cemetery Hill with Union artillery in their hands.

On the slope below, Colonel Isaac Avery was shot through the neck. He knew he was dying. Unable to speak, he found a pencil and a scrap of paper and wrote with a shaking hand: 'Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy.'

Then he wrote his father's name, and died.

On the summit, Carroll's Union brigade counterattacked. Without Confederate infantry support coming behind them, Hays and the survivors of Avery's command could not hold. They came back down the hill in the darkness, back through the town, back to their starting line.

They had touched the crest. They had held the guns. They had come closer to breaking the Union center than any Confederate force at Gettysburg.

But it was not enough."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Lee's report: 'On Cemetery Hill, the attack by Early's leading brigades, those of Hays and Hoke, under Colonel Avery, was made with vigor. Two lines of the enemy's infantry were dislodged from the cover of some stone and board fences on the side of the ascent, and driven back into the works on the crest, into which our troops forced their way, and seized several pieces of artillery. A heavy force advanced against their right, which was without support, and they were compelled to retire, bringing with them about 100 prisoners and four stand of colors.' Rodes was not in position to co-operate, and Early retired for want of the expected support.

Colonel Avery, commanding Hoke's North Carolina brigade, was mortally wounded in the attack. The note he is said to have written, 'Tell my father I died with my face to the enemy', is traditional; the usual account has it written in pencil on a scrap of paper, not in blood.

On the Union side Carroll's brigade of the II Corps came up and drove the attackers off the hill."
patches.note: contradiction: OR 27/2 p.319 (Lee); the note is tradition and labelled

patches.find: "trigger_tick": 525
patches.repl: "trigger_tick": 521
patches.note: unsupported-quote: Alexander, Military Memoirs of a Confederate (1907), read in the Internet Archive scan militarymemoirso01alex; OR 27/2 p.360 (Longstreet)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "As the Confederate cannonade approached its end, Colonel Edward Porter Alexander sent two messages to General Pickett that define the moment when the charge became inevitable. The first urged haste -- ammunition was nearly gone. The second, the most ominous, told Pickett that Alexander himself would not advise making the charge -- but that the order had been given and the troops were already moving."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Colonel E. P. Alexander, Longstreet's artillery chief, sent two notes to Pickett during the cannonade, by his own later account at 1:25 and 1:40 p.m. The first said Pickett must come at once if he were to advance at all; the second, after Alexander saw Union guns withdraw, said 'For God's sake come quick.' The texts come from Alexander's memoir; the Official Records do not print them."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: Alexander, Military Memoirs of a Confederate (1907), read in the Internet Archive scan militarymemoirso01alex; OR 27/2 p.360 (Longstreet)

patches.find:
"full_script": "Colonel Edward Porter Alexander was twenty-eight years old, the chief of artillery for Longstreet's corps, and the man responsible for directing the greatest artillery bombardment in the history of the Western Hemisphere.

For two hours, 170 Confederate guns had been firing at Cemetery Ridge. The Union guns had fallen mostly silent. To Alexander, watching from Seminary Ridge through the smoke and dust, it looked like the cannonade might have worked. The ridge appeared quieter.

But Alexander was running out of ammunition. The Confederate army had no ammunition reserve close enough to replenish the batteries before the infantry assault. When the guns stopped firing, there would be nothing left for close support.

He wrote his first message to Pickett:

'General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or I cannot give you proper support, but the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and at least eighteen guns are still firing from the Cemetery itself.'

Pickett showed the message to Longstreet. Longstreet, who had spent two days arguing against this assault, could not speak. He bowed his head.

Alexander watched the ridge. The Union guns were still silent. He wrote a second message:

'For God's sake come quick. The eighteen guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition won't let me support you properly.'

Pickett came to Longstreet. 'General, shall I advance?'

Longstreet turned away. He could not order it. He bowed his head again.

Pickett understood. He rode to his division.

Alexander never forgot what he had done. In his memoir, written decades later, he wrote that when he sent that first message he had not understood what he was setting in motion -- that he was, in effect, writing the death warrant for thousands of men. If he had known the ammunition supply was nearly gone, he wrote, he would have urged Longstreet to stop the assault entirely.

'I would not make the charge now,' he had written in a later message. 'But the order has been given and the troops are already moving.'

They were."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Alexander, who directed the Confederate guns, wrote in 1907 that he sent this note to Pickett at 1:25: "General: If you are to advance at all, you must come at once or we will not be able to support you as we ought. But the enemy's fire has not slackened materially and there are still 18 guns firing from the cemetery."

He had hardly sent it when he saw the Union fire fall off and guns limbered up and withdrawn. At 1:40, he writes, he sent another: "For God's sake come quick. The 18 guns have gone. Come quick or my ammunition will not let me support you properly." Alexander says he later learned that the first note reached Pickett in Longstreet's presence; Pickett handed it to Longstreet, who stood silent and turned away, and Pickett said, 'I am going to move forward, sir.'

Longstreet's own report says he found that Alexander had advised Pickett that the time had come, gave Pickett the order to advance, and found the supply of ammunition so short that the batteries could not reopen. Words once printed here as Alexander's, 'I would not make the charge now', are not in his memoir."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: Alexander, Military Memoirs of a Confederate (1907), read in the Internet Archive scan militarymemoirso01alex; OR 27/2 p.360 (Longstreet)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Brigadier General Lewis Armistead placed his hat on his sword as a guide and led his brigade over the stone wall at The Angle -- the deepest Confederate penetration of the battle. He was shot down moments later, falling among Union troops beyond the wall. His old friend Winfield Hancock was wounded simultaneously on the other side of the ridge. Both men lay bleeding at the High Water Mark of the Confederacy."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Brigadier General Lewis Armistead led part of his brigade over the low wall at the Angle, the farthest point the Confederate assault reached. Harrow reports that he was left mortally wounded within the Union lines; Lee's report counted him among the killed, and he died of his wounds in Union hands. Meade reports that Hancock and Gibbon were both severely wounded in the assault."
patches.note: unsupported-detail: OR 27/1 p.374 (Hancock), p.428 (Harrow), p.117 (Meade); OR 27/2 p.321 (Lee)

patches.find:
"full_script": "Lewis Armistead and Winfield Hancock had been friends since before the war -- close friends, the kind of friends that the old army made of men who served together in remote posts for years. When Virginia seceded, Armistead had gone south. On the night before he left California, at a farewell party, he had placed his hands on Hancock's shoulders and wept. 'Hancock, goodbye,' he said. 'You can never know what this has cost me.'

That was two years before Gettysburg.

Now Armistead led what remained of his Virginia brigade across the open ground toward Cemetery Ridge. The cannonade had cleared some of the Union guns. There was a gap -- a real gap -- in the line ahead, near a low stone wall and a copse of trees.

Armistead placed his black felt hat on the tip of his sword, raising it above his head as a guide for his men in the smoke and confusion. He walked forward -- not ran, walked, with a deliberate stride. Ahead was the wall.

He stepped over the wall. Behind him, perhaps 150 men followed.

Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing had been serving his last two guns at that wall all afternoon, wounded twice already, holding the battery together through sheer will. When Armistead's men came over the wall, Cushing was at his gun. He was shot through the mouth and killed.

Armistead reached out and touched one of Cushing's guns. A moment later he was shot -- the exact details are disputed, but he fell within the Union lines, beyond the wall.

He was carried to the Union rear. As he lay dying, he asked for Hancock to be brought to him. He did not know that Hancock, on the other side of the ridge, had been wounded almost simultaneously -- a nail and saddle pommel fragment driven deep into his thigh.

Both men lay bleeding. The Confederacy had reached its High Water Mark.

Armistead died two days later. He never saw Hancock again.

The stone wall at The Angle, the copse of trees behind it, and the ground where Armistead fell are preserved today exactly as they were on the afternoon of July 3, 1863. A monument marks the spot where he went down."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Hancock reports that when the enemy's line 'had nearly reached the stone wall, led by General Armistead, the most of that part of Webb's brigade posted here abandoned their position' but 'did not retreat entirely'; Webb and his officers formed them behind the crest. 'The enemy's battle-flags were soon seen waving on the stone wall', and numbers of Confederates crossed the breastwork the troops had left. Colonel Devereux's 19th Massachusetts and Colonel Mallon's 42nd New York were sent to the point, and after a few moments of desperate fighting the Confederates were repulsed.

Harrow writes that 'General Armistead was left, mortally wounded, within my lines, and 42 of the enemy who crossed the fence lay dead.' Armistead and Hancock had been friends in the old army, and the farewell scene and Armistead's request to be brought to Hancock are told in later memoirs, as is the hat raised on his sword; none is in the reports. Meade reports that Hancock and Gibbon were both severely wounded during the assault.

The Angle, the copse of trees and the stone wall are preserved, and monuments mark the field."
patches.note: unsupported-detail: OR 27/1 p.374 (Hancock), p.428 (Harrow), p.117 (Meade); OR 27/2 p.321 (Lee)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "At approximately 1:00pm on July 3, two Confederate signal guns fired in sequence and 170 guns erupted along Seminary Ridge -- the largest artillery bombardment ever seen on the North American continent. The sound was heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away. Alexander's guns fired for nearly two hours before Pickett stepped off."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "About 1 p.m. on July 3 the Confederate batteries opened together on the Union center and left at a given signal. Lee gives the hour as about 1 p.m.; Meade speaks of over 125 guns, Hunt of 100 to 120 bearing on the Union front, Pendleton of nearly 150 in position. The Union guns, about 80 in action by Hunt's count, withheld their fire through the first burst and then replied."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.320 (Lee), p.352 (Pendleton); OR 27/1 p.117 (Meade), p.239-240 (Hunt); ledger WSD-15, WSD-16

patches.find:
"full_script": "At one o'clock in the afternoon, two signal guns fired from Seminary Ridge.

Then 170 guns fired at once.

The sound was heard in Pittsburgh. Some accounts place it as far as Philadelphia -- 140 miles to the east. The smoke rising from Seminary Ridge was visible for twenty miles. Every gun in Alexander's command, every gun in the Third Corps artillery, every piece that could bear on Cemetery Ridge fired simultaneously and continued firing.

Alexander had positioned his guns with extraordinary care. They stretched for nearly two miles along Seminary Ridge, wheel to wheel in places, the barrels elevated slightly to reach the distant blue line on Cemetery Ridge. The Washington Artillery of New Orleans -- the most famous artillery unit in the Confederate army -- was in the line. Pegram's battalion fired from the northern end. Cabell's and Henry's battalions fired from the south.

On Cemetery Ridge, the Union infantry pressed themselves flat behind the stone walls and into the shallow hollows and swales of the ground. The Confederate fire was intense but, as Hunt had feared, much of it was overshooting -- landing behind the ridge near the Taneytown Road, destroying caissons and limbers, killing horses and headquarters staff, nearly hitting Meade himself.

Hunt watched the fire carefully. He began deliberately silencing the Union guns -- battery by battery, pulling them back or having them cease fire. He was conserving ammunition for what he knew was coming. Hancock, riding the line and watching his infantry press closer to the ground, overruled him on some batteries: keep firing, he said. The men need to see their guns fighting.

For nearly two hours the ground shook.

Then Alexander sent his first message to Pickett.

And then the guns fell silent, and across the open fields of Pennsylvania, 12,500 men in gray and butternut stepped out of the tree line and began to walk east."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Lee's report: 'About 1 p. m., at a given signal, a heavy cannonade was opened.' Meade's report: 'the enemy opened from over one hundred and twenty-five guns, playing upon our center and left'. Hunt estimated 'the number of his guns bearing on our west front at from one hundred to one hundred and twenty', quoting enemy correspondents for 115, and writes that 'to oppose these we could not, from our restricted position, bring more than eighty to reply effectively'. Pendleton counts 'nearly one hundred and fifty' of the Confederate guns in position.

Hunt held the Union fire through the first burst and then opened 'deliberately and with excellent effect'. Many Confederate shells passed over the crest and fell among the horses, caissons and limbers behind it. About 2:30, with ammunition running low, Hunt had the fire gradually stopped, and Meade reports that the Union guns, in obedience to his orders, failed to reply.

A later account says Hunt and Hancock disagreed over whether to keep firing; it is not in the reports. Claims that this was the largest bombardment ever heard in the hemisphere, or that it was heard in Philadelphia, are not in the Official Records."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.320 (Lee), p.352 (Pendleton); OR 27/1 p.117 (Meade), p.239-240 (Hunt); ledger WSD-15, WSD-16

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing served his last two guns at The Angle through the Confederate cannonade and Pickett's assault, twice wounded but refusing to leave. He was killed while firing at Armistead's men crossing the wall -- shot through the mouth. He received the Medal of Honor in 2014, 151 years after his death -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing commanded Battery A, 4th U.S. Artillery (six 3-inch rifles) at the Angle. Webb reports that he fought for an hour and a half after reporting that he was wounded in both thighs, and was killed at the fence by the side of his guns; Hunt lists him among the battery commanders killed. He was awarded the Medal of Honor in 2014."
patches.note: unsupported-detail: OR 27/1 p.239-240 (Hunt), p.429 (Webb), p.437

patches.find:
"full_script": "Alonzo Cushing was twenty-two years old.

He had graduated from West Point in 1861 and commanded Battery A, 4th US Artillery -- six three-inch rifles positioned directly behind the stone wall at The Angle, at the exact focal point of the Confederate assault.

The cannonade had been brutal for his battery. Horses killed. Men down. Two of his six guns disabled. By the time Pickett's infantry appeared at the tree line, Cushing had four guns serviceable and was wounded himself -- a fragment through the shoulder.

As the Confederate line crossed the Emmitsburg Road and came on, Cushing took another hit. The wound was grave -- a shell fragment through the groin. His sergeant, Frederick Fuger, urged him to go to the rear.

Cushing refused. He had two guns left. He would serve them himself.

With Fuger's help, he moved his last two guns to the wall itself -- the stone wall at The Angle -- and loaded them with double canister. As Armistead's men climbed over the wall on his left, as the Union line bent and buckled around him, Cushing fired one last round of canister into the Confederate infantry at a range of perhaps twenty yards.

He was shot through the mouth.

Fuger assumed command of what remained of the battery. The Angle held.

Cushing's family petitioned for a Medal of Honor for the next century and a half. The Army reviewed the case repeatedly. Bureaucratic obstacles -- the statute of limitations, administrative requirements -- delayed the award for generations.

On November 6, 2014, President Obama presented the Medal of Honor to a descendant of Cushing's family at a White House ceremony. Alonzo Cushing received the nation's highest military honor 151 years after he died earning it -- the longest gap between action and award in the history of the decoration.

He was twenty-two years old."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Hunt's report counts Cushing's battery among those that 'had lost heavily in men and horses', with Cushing among the three battery commanders killed in the day's fighting. Webb, commanding the brigade he supported, writes: 'Lieut. A. H. Cushing, Fourth U. S. Artillery, fell, mortally wounded, at the fence by the side of his guns. Cool, brave, competent, he fought for an hour and a half after he had reported to me that he was wounded in both thighs.'

Another officer reports that Cushing 'challenged the admiration of all who saw him': three limbers blown up and replaced with caisson limbers under fire, wheels shot off and replaced, until, 'severely wounded himself, his officers all killed or wounded, and with but cannoneers enough to man a section, he pushed his gun to the fence in front, and was killed while serving his last canister into the ranks' of the enemy.

The story that he was shot through the mouth, and details of his sergeant's part, come from later accounts. Cushing was awarded the Medal of Honor in 2014 after a long campaign by his family and supporters."
patches.note: unsupported-detail: OR 27/1 p.239-240 (Hunt), p.429 (Webb), p.437

patches.find:
"title": "Pickett's Return",
      "trigger_tick": 556
patches.repl:
"title": "Pickett's Return",
      "trigger_tick": 557
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.339 (page image: Pickett's division 232 / 1,157 / 1,499 = 2,888), p.321 (Lee)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "After the repulse of Pickett's Charge, Lee rode forward to meet his broken men and told them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' General Pickett, asked by Lee to reform his division for defense, replied: 'General Lee, I have no division.' Pickett never forgave Lee for ordering the charge and never recovered from the loss of his men."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "After the repulse Pickett's division came back across the fields. The Confederate return counts 2,888 casualties in it, 1,499 of them captured or missing (OR 27/2 p.339); Lee reports that Armistead and Garnett were killed and Kemper dangerously wounded. Pickett's remark that he had no division is a tradition from later accounts."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.339 (page image: Pickett's division 232 / 1,157 / 1,499 = 2,888), p.321 (Lee)

patches.find:
"full_script": "George Pickett sat on his horse and watched his division come back.

They came in clusters and straggles, the survivors of a mile-wide charge across open ground under artillery and musketry. Some walked steadily. Some stumbled. Some were helping others walk. All of them had the look of men who had been through something that no words could explain.

Of the three brigades Pickett had sent forward -- Garnett, Kemper, Armistead -- Garnett was dead, Kemper was critically wounded and briefly a prisoner, Armistead was dying beyond the stone wall he had crossed. The division had suffered nearly 2,700 casualties from 5,500 engaged. Forty-nine percent.

Lee rode forward to meet them.

He rode along the broken line, and he said to them, over and over, the same thing: 'It is all my fault. It is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.'

Pickett came to Lee. Lee told him to reform his division -- there might be a Union counterattack coming.

Pickett looked at Lee. 'General Lee,' he said, 'I have no division.'

Lee never acknowledged, officially or privately, that ordering the charge had been a mistake. He praised the courage of his men and said that more support should have been provided. In his official report he blamed himself in the most general terms.

Pickett blamed Lee specifically. For the rest of his life he told anyone who would listen that Lee had destroyed his division. When someone praised Lee in Pickett's presence years after the war, Pickett said quietly: 'That man destroyed my division.'

He said it with the measured tone of a man who had been carrying the weight of it for decades."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "The Confederate return of casualties gives Pickett's division 232 killed, 1,157 wounded and 1,499 captured or missing, 2,888 in all: Garnett's brigade 941, Armistead's 1,191, Kemper's 731, and the artillery battalion 25. The division's strength is not printed in the reports read here, so a percentage is not given.

Lee's report says: 'The troops were rallied and reformed, but the enemy did not pursue. A large number of brave officers and men fell or were captured on this occasion. Of Pickett's three brigade commanders, Generals Armistead and Garnett were killed, and General Kemper dangerously wounded.'

A well-known exchange in which Lee asked Pickett to re-form his division and Pickett answered that he had no division, and later reports of Pickett's bitterness toward Lee, come from memoirs and recollections, not from the Official Records."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/2 p.339 (page image: Pickett's division 232 / 1,157 / 1,499 = 2,888), p.321 (Lee)
