patches.find: "panel_summary": "Three miles east of Gettysburg, while Pickett's infantry was being repulsed at The Angle, Stuart's cavalry attempted to sweep around the Union rear. The 23-year-old General George Armstrong Custer personally led the Michigan Brigade in a mounted charge that stopped Stuart cold. 'Come on, you Wolverines!' he shouted -- and they came."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "East of Gettysburg on the afternoon of July 3 Stuart's cavalry met Gregg's division and Custer's Michigan Brigade while the infantry assault was made at the center. Lee's report says the cavalry 'effectually protected our left' and that Hampton was seriously wounded. The hour of the main charges (about 3 p.m. by one account) and Custer's reported shout are from later accounts."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/2 p.322 (Lee); time-facts R119, R120

patches.find:
"full_script": "George Armstrong Custer was twenty-three years old and had been a brigadier general for exactly eight days.

He had earned the promotion through a combination of extraordinary courage and extraordinary luck -- the kind of officer who seemed to attract bullets that always missed. He wore a custom uniform of black velvet with gold trim that made him conspicuous on any battlefield. He wore his hair in long golden ringlets. He was, in the Army of the Potomac, impossible to ignore.

On the afternoon of July 3, while Pickett's infantry was crossing the open fields toward Cemetery Ridge, Stuart's cavalry moved east of Gettysburg to sweep around the Union rear. If Stuart could strike the Union rear simultaneously with the infantry assault on the front, the Army of the Potomac might be destroyed.

Gregg's cavalry division blocked the road. Custer's Michigan Brigade -- 1,900 troopers on fresh horses -- was the striking force.

Stuart advanced. Hampton's South Carolinians and Fitz Lee's Virginians moved forward in what Confederate veterans later described as a magnificent charge -- thousands of horsemen covering the ground in a sweeping wall of cavalry.

Custer rode to the front of his brigade. He turned to his Wolverines.

'Come on, you Wolverines!'

He spurred his horse directly at the Confederate advance. The Michigan Brigade came with him.

The two lines met at a full gallop in the largest cavalry engagement of the Gettysburg campaign. Men sabre'd each other at close range, horses went down, the lines interpenetrated and dissolved into a melee of individual combats across a half-mile front. Hampton was wounded -- a sabre cut to the head.

When it was over, Stuart's cavalry fell back. The Union rear was secure.

On Cemetery Ridge, the last of Pickett's men were streaming back from The Angle.

Custer had done his part."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Lee's report says Stuart arrived on the afternoon of July 2 and took position on Ewell's left, and that 'the day after its arrival at Gettysburg it engaged the enemy's cavalry with unabated spirit, and effectually protected our left. In this action, Brigadier-General Hampton was seriously wounded, while acting with his accustomed gallantry.'

Gregg's division and Custer's Michigan Brigade held the ground east of the town. The fight began in the early afternoon (accounts put the opening between about 1 and 2:30 p.m.), and the climax, in which Hampton's brigade charged and Custer led the 1st Michigan against it, is dated about 3 p.m. in one account.

Custer was commissioned a brigadier general in late June; the length of his rank at the time, once given here as 'exactly eight days', is not stated in the sources read. His shout, 'Come on, you Wolverines!', is from veterans' later accounts, as is the size of his brigade."
patches.note: wrong-claim: OR 27/2 p.322 (Lee); time-facts R119, R120

patches.find: "panel_summary": "General Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days when Kilpatrick ordered him to charge Confederate infantry over rocky terrain south of the battlefield. Farnsworth protested that the charge was suicidal. Kilpatrick insisted. Farnsworth led the charge and was killed. He had been a general for exactly four days when he died."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "About 5 p.m. on July 3 Kilpatrick ordered Farnsworth's brigade to charge on the Confederate right south of the Round Tops, and Farnsworth was killed leading it. Farnsworth had been a brigadier general since June 29. Reports that he protested, and the words said to have passed between him and Kilpatrick, come from survivors' later accounts."
patches.note: contradiction: time-facts R122, triage (promotion June 29); the quotations are labelled later accounts

patches.find:
"full_script": "Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days.

He had the promotion because he was a good cavalry officer and because his uncle was an influential congressman and because Pleasonton was promoting young men he trusted. Eight days -- long enough to receive the commission, pin on the stars, and die.

Kilpatrick ordered him to charge.

Farnsworth looked at the ground ahead. It was a nightmare of boulders and fencing and rocky terrain, defended by Law's Confederate infantry and the dismounted men of Robertson's Texas Brigade. Cavalry -- even the best cavalry -- could not charge formed infantry over ground like that.

He said so.

Kilpatrick, in the accounts that survive, challenged his courage. The exact words are disputed, but the meaning was clear: charge, or be thought a coward.

Farnsworth's face went white. Then he said something that the men nearby remembered for the rest of their lives -- an expression of outrage, of contempt, and of acceptance, all in one breath. He would lead the charge himself.

'If you order the charge, I will lead it,' he said. 'But if we go in there it will be a charge of death.'

Kilpatrick ordered the charge.

Farnsworth rode to the front of his brigade and led them forward into the rocks and the Confederate fire.

He was shot five times. He fell among the boulders south of Big Round Top, a general for four days.

The charge accomplished nothing. No Confederate position was taken, no Union position was relieved. The men who survived came back to their starting line having given nothing and gained nothing.

Kilpatrick's decision was condemned then and has been condemned since. He spent the rest of his life defending it."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Farnsworth had been promoted to brigadier general on June 29, four days before the charge. The ABT map dates the action to the south cavalry field at about 5:15 to 6 p.m.

Kilpatrick ordered the charge against Confederate infantry on the right of Lee's line, south and east of Big Round Top, over rocky, fenced ground. Survivors later said that Farnsworth objected and that Kilpatrick answered sharply; the exact words are disputed and are not repeated here. Farnsworth led the brigade forward and was killed. The charge gained no ground.

The question of whether the order was justified has been argued ever since; the reports read here do not settle it."
patches.note: contradiction: time-facts R122, triage (promotion June 29); the quotations are labelled later accounts

patches.find: "panel_summary": "Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge was ordered to lead his 2nd Massachusetts Infantry in a charge across open ground toward Confederate positions at Culp's Hill. He protested the order. When told it was confirmed, he said: 'It is murder but it is the order.' He led the charge and was killed instantly. The regiment suffered 43% casualties in minutes."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "On the morning of July 3 Colonel Colgrove sent the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana across the open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks on Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded, including its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Mudge, and the 27th Indiana 112. The hour is disputed and Mudge's reported last words come from survivors' later accounts."
patches.note: wrong-time: OR 27/1 p.813-814 (Colgrove), p.782 (Williams), p.816 (Fesler: killed 18, wounded 93)

patches.find:
"full_script": "The order came down at approximately 7:30 in the morning of July 3.

Colonize Silas Colgrove had received instructions to clear Confederate infantry from their position at the base of Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana were to charge across an open meadow -- perhaps 200 yards of ground fully exposed to Confederate fire from the woods beyond.

Lieutenant Colonel Charles Mudge commanded the 2nd Massachusetts. He read the order and then read it again.

He sent an aide back to Colgrove. Was the order correct? Had there been a mistake?

The aide came back. The order was confirmed.

Mudge looked at the meadow. He looked at his regiment -- 316 men who had served through two years of war, who had marched from Maryland to Pennsylvania, who trusted him.

He turned to his officers.

'It is murder,' he said. 'But it is the order.'

He drew his saber and led the 2nd Massachusetts across the meadow at the double-quick.

The Confederate fire from the woods was immediate and accurate. Men fell as they ran. Mudge was hit almost at once -- shot through the throat, killed instantly, falling in the open ground he had called murder to cross.

The regiment reached the Confederate position, could not hold it, and withdrew. In the few minutes of the charge and its aftermath, 136 of 316 men were casualties -- 43 percent.

The 27th Indiana charged alongside them. It did not go better.

Colgrove's charge is still debated. Some accounts suggest the order was given in confusion, that it was never meant to be a frontal assault across open ground. Whatever the intent, the result was exactly what Mudge had predicted.

His last words -- 'It is murder but it is the order' -- are among the most quoted of the battle."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "Colonel Silas Colgrove's report says that after about two hours of sharpshooter fire from daylight, the firing on his left receded and he heard cheering; Geary's division had retaken its breastworks. A staff officer then brought the order, 'The general directs that you advance your line immediately.' Between his line and the enemy lay 'the open meadow, about 100 yards in width', and the enemy were sheltered by breastworks and ledges of rock.

He chose the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana. 'At the command, "Forward, double-quick!" our breastworks were cleared, and both regiments, with deafening cheers, sprang forward. They had scarcely gained the open ground when they were met with one of the most terrible fires I have ever witnessed ... It became evident to me that scarcely a man could live to gain the position of the enemy.' The 27th Indiana was ordered back behind the breastworks and the 2nd Massachusetts, overpowered, fell back too; then the Confederates charged and were broken by the fire from the works.

'In the charge, the Second Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded. Among the killed was its commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Mudge, who fell while gallantly leading his men.' The 27th Indiana lost 112 killed and wounded. The hour is disputed (about two hours after daylight in Colgrove's report; the forenoon in Williams's; later in other accounts). Mudge's reported words, 'It is murder, but it is the order', are from survivors' recollections, not the reports."
patches.note: wrong-time: OR 27/1 p.813-814 (Colgrove), p.782 (Williams), p.816 (Fesler: killed 18, wounded 93)

patches.find: "panel_summary": "As the survivors of Pickett's Charge streamed back toward Seminary Ridge, Robert E. Lee rode out to meet them personally, telling them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' Imboden, who was with Lee that evening, described him pacing back and forth saying 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.' It was the closest Lee ever came to public acknowledgment of error."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "As the survivors of the assault came back toward Seminary Ridge, Lee rode out to meet them. Lee's report says the troops were rallied and re-formed and the enemy did not pursue. The words reported from him, such as 'It is all my fault', come from witnesses' later accounts, among them Imboden's postwar article."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/2 p.321 (Lee); the quoted accounts are labelled later

patches.find:
"full_script": "General John Imboden had been ordered to prepare for the retreat. He was waiting near Lee's headquarters when the survivors of Pickett's Charge began coming back across the fields.

Lee rode out to meet them.

He rode slowly along the broken line of men, and Imboden watched from nearby. What he saw, he wrote later, he never forgot.

Lee rode among his men and said to them, over and over: 'All this has been my fault -- it is I who have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it the best you can.' Some of the men reached up and touched his boots as he passed. Some wept.

When Pickett came to him, Lee said: 'Come, General Pickett. This has been my fight, and upon my shoulders rests the blame.'

That night, Lee found Imboden waiting for him.

'General,' Imboden said, 'this has been a hard day on you.'

Lee said nothing at first. He sat on his horse in the darkness. Then he began to talk, and Imboden wrote down what he said as carefully as he could remember:

'I never saw troops behave more magnificently than Pickett's division of Virginians did today in that grand charge upon the enemy. And if they had been supported as they were to have been -- but for some reason not yet fully explained -- the charge would have been gloriously successful.'

Then Lee fell silent again. He seemed to be speaking almost to himself.

'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

Imboden heard him say it over and over as they rode back toward headquarters.

Lee never said it quite so plainly again."
patches.repl: "full_script": "Lee's report says of the repulse: 'The troops were rallied and reformed, but the enemy did not pursue.' It says nothing of what he said to the men. In later accounts several witnesses report that he met the survivors, took blame on himself, and said that Pickett's division had behaved magnificently; Imboden, who wrote of a conversation with Lee that night, quoted him as saying 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'\n\nImboden's account was published in the 1880s, and the wording differs between witnesses. They are given here as reported, not as documented."
patches.note: unsupported-quote: OR 27/2 p.321 (Lee); the quoted accounts are labelled later

patches.find: "panel_summary": "The Battle of Gettysburg ended on July 3, 1863 with approximately 51,000 casualties across three days -- the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. The spot where Armistead fell at The Angle is marked today as the High Water Mark of the Confederacy. The Army of Northern Virginia would never again invade the North."
patches.repl: "panel_summary": "The Battle of Gettysburg ended on July 3, 1863. The Official Records give the Union loss as 23,049 (revised return) and the Confederate loss as 20,451 as returned, a return the editors call approximate; later estimates run higher, the National Park Service giving about 23,000 Union and 28,000 Confederate. Lee began the withdrawal on July 4."
patches.note: wrong-number: OR 27/1 p.187; OR 27/2 p.322, p.346; ledger WSD-01, WSD-02; NPS Battle Detail (about 23,000 and 28,000); the 1,328 is the NPS-wide count named in docs/plan findings (data-integrity-29), distinct from the 512 monuments of the app

patches.find:
"full_script": "The battle was over.

From the first shot on Knoxlyn Ridge on the morning of July 1 to the last cavalry action east of town on the afternoon of July 3, the Battle of Gettysburg had consumed three days and approximately 51,000 men. Seven thousand were dead. The rest were wounded or missing. The fields and orchards and woodlots of Adams County, Pennsylvania -- farmland, ordinary farmland -- were covered with the wreckage of two armies.

On July 4, while the town of Gettysburg tried to count its dead, the news arrived from the west: Vicksburg had fallen. Grant had split the Confederacy. Two disasters in two days.

Lee began his retreat on July 4 in a driving rainstorm. Imboden's wagon train -- seventeen miles of it, filled with wounded men who screamed with every jolt of the road -- moved south and west toward Virginia. The army followed, battered, depleted, but intact. Meade chose not to pursue aggressively. The opportunity to destroy Lee's army, if it existed, was not taken.

The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years. There would be Cold Harbor and the Wilderness and Petersburg and the Shenandoah and Appomattox. But the moment when Confederate victory was possible -- the moment when a successful invasion of the North might have forced a negotiated peace -- had passed on the afternoon of July 3 at a stone wall in Pennsylvania.

The copse of trees still stands. The stone wall has been rebuilt where it was torn apart in the fighting. A bronze marker -- placed by veterans, not the government -- stands near the spot where Armistead fell.

It reads: 'The High Water Mark of the Rebellion.'

The ground is quiet now. The fields are green in summer, brown in fall, white in winter. The monuments stand in long rows along Seminary Ridge and Cemetery Ridge and the slopes of Culp's Hill and Little Round Top. There are 1,328 of them -- more monuments per square mile than anywhere else on earth.

In July, when the heat is heavy and the air still, you can stand at The Angle and look west across the open fields and understand exactly what happened here, and why it mattered, and what it cost."
patches.repl:
"full_script": "The battle was over. The Official Records print the Union loss for the campaign as 23,049 killed, wounded and missing in the revised return (3,155 killed, 14,529 wounded, 5,365 captured or missing), and the Confederate loss as returned as 20,451 (2,592 killed, 12,709 wounded, 5,150 captured or missing), which the editors call approximate. Later estimates are higher, notably Livermore's of about 28,000 for the Confederates, and the National Park Service gives about 23,000 and 28,000. The sum of 51,000 sometimes quoted is that rounded estimate. These counts include the wounded and missing; the figures for the dead alone differ again by source.

On July 4 Vicksburg surrendered. Lee's report says the heavy loss and reduced ammunition made another attack inadvisable and it was determined to withdraw: the trains with the wounded who could bear removal were sent to Williamsport on July 4, part by Cashtown and Greencastle under Imboden and the rest by the Fairfield road, and the army kept its position until dark and then marched in a heavy rain. Meade did not pursue closely.

The park preserves hundreds of monuments and markers; the number quoted in earlier versions of this page, 1,328, is the park's total for all monuments, markers and tablets, not for the monuments mapped here. The Angle and the copse of trees are preserved, and the wall there has been rebuilt."
